Béla Bartók. The Hungarian composer, pianist, and ethnomusicologist from 1881 to 1945, he was one of the most influential figures of twentieth-century music. Alongside Zoltán Kodály, Bartók traveled throughout Eastern Europe, North Africa, and Asia Minor to record and transcribe thousands of peasant folk tunes, co-founding the field of ethnomusicology. His compositions brilliantly synthesize these traditional folk melodies and irregular rhythms with modern Western techniques like atonality, creating a highly personal style marked by driving rhythms, mathematical symmetries, and visceral energy.

His most popular and celebrated orchestral work is the Concerto for Orchestra from 1943, commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky while Bartók was dying of leukemia in American exile. Its fourth movement, Intermezzo interrotto, famously parodies a repetitive theme from Shostakovich's Leningrad Symphony. Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta from 1936 is a masterpiece of complex symmetry that utilizes the Fibonacci sequence and the golden ratio to determine its structural climaxes. The slow third movement is a prime example of his atmospheric night music style. Duke Bluebeard's Castle from 1911 is his sole opera, a dark, symbolist one-act work setting a Hungarian libretto in which Judith insists on opening seven locked doors inside the castle of her new husband Bluebeard, discovering blood behind each door.

Mikrokosmos spans from 1926 to 1939 and is a pedagogical monument consisting of one hundred fifty-three piano pieces arranged in six volumes of progressive difficulty. It was designed to introduce students to modern piano technique and musical concepts. His six string quartets are considered by musicologists to be the most important string quartet cycle written since Beethoven's. They utilize innovative string techniques like the Bartók snap, a snap pizzicato where the string rebounds violently off the fingerboard. The Miraculous Mandarin from 1926 is a scandalous pantomime ballet about a gang of thieves who use a young woman to lure men to be robbed and killed. A wealthy Mandarin survives hanging and stabbing out of sheer lust for the girl until his desire is finally satiated.

Bartók stands as a titan of early twentieth-century European modernism alongside Stravinsky and Schoenberg. He drew inspiration from Stravinsky's rhythmic drive and primitive aesthetics, especially in his own early works. In his Concerto for Orchestra, he parodied Shostakovich's Leningrad Symphony to mock its repetitive, overhyped nature.
